newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Fighting breaks out again on approaches to Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Fighting breaks out again on approaches to Kabul.

text.p: Renewed fighting for control of the heights above Kabul broke out on Wednesday after a brief lull gave scores of villagers the chance to escape the combat zone.
Fighters for the Taleban Islamic militia on the front line said there had been a break since dawn in their battle with the forces of ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.
"But there isn't a ceasefire. We'll be starting again soon," said one.

Minutes later, Taleban artillery and mortars opened up on Masood's positions on and around the main road north from Kabul, where the front lines do not appear to have shifted significantly in the past few days despite claims of gains by both sides.
The Taleban seized control of Kabul on September 27 and are believed to control three-quarters of the country.

On the Masood side of the front line Reuters correspondent Chris Bird reported that forces loyal to Masood launched a heavy attack on Wednesday morning on Taleban positions at the village of Kalakan, which is about 25 km (18 miles) north of Kabul.
"We are moving around to encircle them and we will move on Kabul, God willing," said Ustod Rahim, one of Masood's commanders.
The shelling was particularly heavy on the so-called new road which leads into northeastern Kabul.
Taleban fighters said their target was to retake Bagram airbase, 50 km (30 miles) north of the capital, in a push up the new road, which runs parallel to the main route.

Before the new bout of fighting erupted women clad in the all-embracing burqa made mandatory by the purist Taleban carried bundles on their heads, children bore smaller children and boys and men drove heavily-laden donkeys as they fled towards Kabul.

Several trucks loaded with bundles and people made the same journey past villages pulverised in days of fighting around the village of Hussein Kot on a dusty plain with the snow-capped Hindu Kush mountains in the background.

Masood, strengthened by an alliance with northern Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum who has sent tanks, artillery and men to the front lines, has called for the demilitarisation of Kabul, ravaged by four years of factional fighting.
But Taleban leader Mullah Mohammad Omar told the Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) agency on Tuesday that his movement would defend the capital.
"Our forces are not in Kabul," the 38-year-old leader said. "All our forces are outside, defending the city. Police control security in Kabul."
However, Taleban fighters, wearing their trademark black turbans and driving around in the only modern vehicles to be seen in the capital, were still numerous on Wednesday.
Omar also told the Pakistan-based AIP he accepted proposals to form a joint commission comprising the Taleban and opposing factions to monitor a ceasefire.
"We don't reject a guarantor role for the United Nations and the Organisation of Islamic Conference," he said.
In New York on Tuesday, the U.N. Security Council called unanimously for a ceasefire and political negotiations in Afghanistan.
U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said if a ceasefire were established, the international community should have a larger presence, with military or civilian observers as a minimum.
Taleban fighters on the front line said they had heard all the talk about a ceasefire.
"But they don't want to stop fighting," said one with a nod towards Masood's positions.
"We'll go on fighting, too, and we'll push them back to where they came from," he added in a reference to Masood's Panjsher valley stronghold from which he counter-attacked 10 days ago.
